comments.author: SmoggySPECTEREGaming
comments.body:
Hey OP! I am in the same boat. There is a lot of trial and error, and learning on the fly. Just because someone inputs a prompt doesn't mean you'll have a complete system working end to end the way it's intended. I still fight with my systems. I resolve errors, I clearly, and specifically define parameters. I copy+paste the code output and let the LLM know that I need this and that iteration or that this feature did not work as intended. Slowly but surely, things start weaving and working together. 

I know a crap tonne more now about Unity than when I first started. I use free assets in the Unity Store or Meshy/Tripo for generating assets. I still have to learn Blender workflow on how to animate them, but I am determined to finish my project.

The most important thing is remembering that no matter what you ship, AI or not, must be quality. People don't want cheap, and rushed. They want immersion. They want fun. They want engaging gameplay. If you can provide that, people stop caring how it was made, just that they want more.

TLDR; just do it. Make mistakes. Ask questions. Look at what others have done. ChatGPT is good at compehension and expanding on your ideas. Claude is good for coding. Meshy/tripo for quick custom asset generation. Get started. Make mistakes, and settle in for the long haul. Just because you are using AI, does not mean it's easy or quick.

comments.author: Happy-Fruit-8628
comments.body: Bigger games usually fail because of scope, not tooling. AI can help generate prototypes or rough systems quickly, but large games still require structure, modular design, and a clear gameplay loop. Use AI to test ideas faster not to skip learning fundamentals.

replies.author: Happy-Fruit-8628
replies.body: Mostly the usual coding assistants like ChatGPT/Copilot. There are also some newer prompt-based prototypes like Tesana experimenting with world generation, but they’re still early compared to traditional engines. AI right now feels strongest at reducing setup time, not replacing full development.

replies.author: Thronebornn
replies.body: Yeah scope is the real problem.

comments.author: SproutsJeremy
comments.body:
I started off by following youtube tutorial series playlists on how to create games. After that I took premade game system packs off the marketplace and modified them to make my game. 

A few years later and I knew the basics of how to make any game I wanted. Or if I didn’t, I knew how to find materials that would allow me to easily. 

With bigger games you might have to bite the bullet and learn how to code and create a game without AI first

comments.author: Pure-Artichoke-4589
comments.body:
AI is just a tool — kind of a half-automated one. It can do simple things pretty well, but once things get more dynamic, you still have to guide it yourself. 

Stuff usually gets built step by step. 



If you’re not sure what to do, just share some ideas and let it try

Then see how it turns out, give feedback, and keep improving it little by little

But this really only works for simple games.
